fetched_contents.text: Vitamins and minerals for subfertility in women Review question: Do supplementary oral antioxidants compared with placebo, with no treatment/standard treatment or with another antioxidant improve fertility outcomes for subfertile women? 'Standard treatment' includes less than 1 mg of folic acid. Background: Many subfertile women undergoing fertility treatment also take dietary supplements in the hope of improving their fertility. This can be a very stressful time for women and their partners. It is important that these couples are given high-quality evidence that will allow them to make informed decisions on whether taking a supplemental antioxidant when undergoing fertility treatment will improve their chances or cause any adverse effects. This is especially important, as most antioxidant supplements are uncontrolled by regulation. This review aimed to assess whether supplements with oral antioxidants increase a subfertile woman's chances of becoming pregnant and having a baby. Search date: The evidence is current to September 2019. Study characteristics: The review includes 63 randomised controlled trials that compare antioxidants with placebo or with no treatment/standard treatment, or with another antioxidant, in a total of 7760 women. Funding sources: Funding sources were reported by only 27 of the 63 included trials. Key results: We are uncertain whether the use of antioxidants will increase live births, as the evidence was of very low quality. Based on our results, we would expect that out of 100 subfertile women not taking antioxidants, 20 would have a baby, compared with between 24 and 36 women per 100 who would have a baby if taking antioxidants. Low-quality evidence suggests that antioxidants may be associated with increased clinical pregnancy rates. Adverse effects were poorly reported, but the use of antioxidants did not appear to lead to more miscarriages, multiple births, digestive effects or ectopic pregnancies. Low-quality evidence suggests that there is no difference in live birth or clinical pregnancy rates when comparing a lower dose of melatonin to a higher dose. Here we would expect that out of 100 subfertile women taking low-dose melatonin, 24 would have a baby, compared with between 12 and 40 women per 100 who would have a baby if taking higher-dose melatonin. Three trials reported on miscarriage in the antioxidant versus antioxidant comparison (two used doses of melatonin and one compared N-acetylcysteine versus L-carnitine). There were no miscarriages in either melatonin trial. Multiple pregnancy and gastrointestinal disturbances were not reported, and ectopic pregnancy was reported by only one trial, with no events. The study comparing N-acetylcysteine with L-carnitine did not report live birth rate. Very low-quality evidence shows no evidence of a difference in clinical pregnancy. Low quality evidence shows no difference in miscarriage. The study did not report multiple pregnancy, gastrointestinal disturbances or ectopic pregnancy. Quality of the evidence: The overall quality of evidence was limited by serious risks of bias associated with poor reporting of methods, imprecision and inconsistency. This may affect up to a quarter of all couples planning a child. It is estimated that for 40% to 50% of couples, subfertility may result from factors affecting women. Antioxidants are thought to reduce the oxidative stress brought on by these conditions. Currently, limited evidence suggests that antioxidants improve fertility, and trials have explored this area with varied results. This review assesses the evidence for the effectiveness of different antioxidants in female subfertility. Objectives To determine whether supplementary oral antioxidants compared with placebo, no treatment/standard treatment or another antioxidant improve fertility outcomes for subfertile women. Search strategy We searched the following databases (from their inception to September 2019), with no language or date restriction: Cochrane Gynaecology and Fertility Group (CGFG) specialised register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, CINAHL and AMED. We checked reference lists of relevant studies and searched the trial registers. Selection criteria We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs) that compared any type, dose or combination of oral antioxidant supplement with placebo, no treatment or treatment with another antioxidant, among women attending a reproductive clinic. fetched_contents.text: The Best Vitamins and Supplements to Boost Your Fertility When trying to conceive, doctors may suggest a variety of things to help optimize one’s health and taking vitamins and supplements is typically on the list. The importance of good nutrition is well established during pregnancy, influencing embryonic and fetal development, and thus, pregnancy outcomes. There is growing evidence that certain supplements and micronutrients may help in many ways for those trying to conceive, including boosting the overall quality of a woman’s eggs and a male’s sperm, as well as the overall health of a woman’s pregnancy. Below, is a list of a few important vitamins and supplements to consider taking when you’re trying to conceive. It’s important to note that you should be receiving many of your daily vitamins and minerals from food sources. But if you have trouble getting all of the recommended daily amounts through food, supplements are a great addition to your diet. Also, women should start taking multivitamins or prenatal vitamins before getting pregnant. In a large scale randomized controlled study, women taking prenatal vitamins at least 1 month before conception were noted to have higher number of confirmed pregnancies and shorter time to conception compared to women only taking trace elements like vitamin C and Zinc. In a large population based observational study, women taking multivitamins or prenatal vitamins had lower incidence of ovulatory infertility. The effect was most prominent with folic acid above 400 ucg at least 3 times a week. If your prenatal vitamin doesn’t include some of these standalone vitamins and supplements, you might want to consider adding a few to your daily intake after consulting a primary care doctor or your fertility doctor to see if these vitamins and supplements are right for you. 1. Folic acid (B9): Most people associate folic acid as a prenatal vitamin, but it can also be a really great supplement for those who are trying to conceive. Folic acid is associated with greater chances of getting pregnant naturally and improves success for those undergoing fertility treatments. Medical professionals also recommend that men take folic acid when trying to conceive, as it can improve the quality of their sperm. Suggested amount: 400-1,000 micrograms for women, 400 micrograms for men. Best form of folic acid is thought to be the methylated folate (quatrefolic). 2. Vitamin B6 and B12: Both are essential nutrients needed for our cells to grow, develop and survive and are important in both men and women. B6 supplementation has been associated with improvement in hormonal balance in women leading to improved PMS symptoms and better ovulatory cycles, which in turn, improved the odds of becoming pregnant. A study in the medical journal Reproductive Toxicology found that those who took supplemental folate and vitamins B6 and B12 lowered their homocysteine levels, which improved the odds of successful conception in women with recurrent pregnancy loss. A separate study conducted in 2017 called “Vitamin B12 and Semen Quality” also found that increased B12 intake in men resulted in improved semen quality. Suggested amount: For B12, 1,000 micrograms once per week for men and women. For B6, 1.4 milligrams for men and 1.2 milligrams for women daily. 3. Myoinositol (B8) and D-chiro-inositol: This is naturally occurring in almost every tissue that is involved in insulin and gonadotropin signaling, affecting follicle maturation. In women with PCOS, myoinositol is associated with improvement in insulin resistance and ovulation. During pregnancy, it may also help prevent gestational diabetes. Suggested amount: 2000 mg two times a day of combination of myoinositol and D-chiroinositol. 4. Vitamin C: Vitamin C is a powerful antioxidant and can promote healthy reproductive systems in both men and women. For women, vitamin C can reduce the negative impact of free radicals, in turn reducing cellular damage, which may then counter aspects of ovarian aging. Research shows vitamin C supplementation is associated with shorter time to pregnancy. As for vitamin C’s impact on male fertility, The Nutrition and Food Security Research Center found that taking vitamin C with vitamin E improved the number, motility, and sometimes DNA quality of sperm. Suggested amount: 90 milligrams minimum daily for men and 75 milligrams minimum daily for women. Liposomal form at 500 mg to 1000 mg or higher doses up to 2000 mg a day is thought to be safe for most adults. 5. Vitamin D: Vitamin D is important for the development of healthy hormones and is thought to play an important role in many chronic diseases from diabetes, autoimmunity, cardiovascular disease and cancer. Those trying to get pregnant can test for vitamin D level to see if they are deficient and start taking supplemental vitamin D if necessary. Sufficient vitamin D level has been associated with improved pregnancy rates. Additionally, this vitamin is thought to improve semen quality in men. Suggested amount: 2,000 to 4,000 international units (IU) daily for men and women. 6. Vitamin E: Most people will recognize vitamin E from their skincare – tons of products include this one to help “reduce wrinkles,” because vitamin E works to prevent cell membrane damage. That’s also exactly what makes it a great vitamin to boost fertility. A study named “Vitamin E as an Antioxidant in Female Reproductive Health” suggests that vitamin E improves women’s overall reproductive health and improves egg quality. For men, it helps to boost sperm quality, and when taken with vitamin C has been shown to reduce DNA fragmentation. fetched_contents.text: Is it Safe to Take Herbal Supplements During Pregnancy? Herbal supplements are increasingly popular with many believing that they are natural alternatives to more conventional medicines commonly prescribed in Western medicine. Unlike prescription drugs, natural herbs and vitamin supplements do not have to go through the rigorous evaluation proving safety and efficacy by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Because of this, the quality and strength of herbal supplements very often vary between two batches of the same product and between products from different manufacturers. Therefore there is no way of knowing the safety of such unregulated products. Many patients ask us, “Is it safe to take herbal supplements during pregnancy?” Even though herbs are natural, not all herbs are safe to take during pregnancy or while trying to become pregnant. Many herbs may have hormone regulatory effects and could cause difficulty conceiving or have harmful effects to pregnancy. Some herbs may even cause miscarriage, premature birth, uterine contractions and injury to the fetus. There are very few studies examining the effects herbs may have on pregnant women and their unborn child. Many herbs such as rosemary and garlic are safe in amounts used customarily in food, medicinal amounts of these same herbs can have uterine stimulatory effects and should be avoided in pregnancy. ## Evidence on which supplements may help fertility

### Which supplements have plausible biological mechanisms for fertility?
The evidence base supports a few supplements based on plausible biological mechanisms, particularly antioxidants and nutrients involved in reproductive health. Cochrane reviews and fertility guides highlight that antioxidants are thought to reduce oxidative stress, which may be relevant to fertility outcomes [N1-F1]. This is why the Cochrane review on vitamins and minerals for female subfertility explicitly included antioxidants and related compounds such as N-acetylcysteine, melatonin, L-arginine, myo-inositol, carnitine, selenium, vitamin E, vitamin B complex, vitamin C, vitamin D+calcium, CoQ10, and omega-3-polyunsaturated fatty acids [N1-F1].

Folic acid also has a clear biological rationale: it is associated with greater chances of getting pregnant naturally and is a core recommendation for women trying to conceive [N2-F2]. Vitamin B6 and B12 are also linked to hormonal balance and ovulatory cycles in women, and some studies suggest they may improve conception odds [N2-F2]. Myo-inositol and D-chiro-inositol are tied to insulin and gonadotropin signaling, affecting follicle maturation and are especially relevant for women with PCOS [N2-F2]. Vitamin C is a powerful antioxidant that may reduce free radical damage and counter aspects of ovarian aging [N2-F2]. Vitamin D is important for hormone development and may improve pregnancy rates, while vitamin E improves reproductive health and egg quality [N2-F2]. CoQ10 is another antioxidant that counters oxidative stress and is promoted for egg and sperm quality [N2-F2].

### Which supplements have moderate evidence for improving pregnancy rates?
The evidence for improving pregnancy rates is more modest than for some of the mechanisms. For antioxidants, the Cochrane review found **low-quality evidence suggesting that antioxidants may improve clinical pregnancy rates compared with placebo or no treatment/standard treatment**, but it was **uncertain whether they improve live birth rates** [N1-F1]. The same review also noted that the evidence was very low quality overall, with serious risks of bias, poor reporting, imprecision, and inconsistency [N1-F1]. A subsequent source also notes that **CoQ10 has shown potential to increase clinical pregnancy rates but has not shown significant increase in live birth rates** [N2-R2].

For folic acid, the evidence is more direct: the Cochrane review explicitly states that **daily folic acid supplementation in ...** is part of the review, and the Progyny guide notes that **folic acid is associated with greater chances of getting pregnant naturally and improves success for those undergoing fertility treatments** [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The evidence for folic acid is therefore stronger than for many antioxidants, though still not a guaranteed fertility guarantee.

For other supplements, the evidence is less robust. The Cochrane review on vitamins and minerals for female subfertility included 63 trials, but the overall quality was very low, and the results were uncertain for live birth and only suggestive for clinical pregnancy [N1-F1]. The evidence on specific supplements such as melatonin, N-acetylcysteine, and L-carnitine is similarly limited by very low quality [N1-F1]. The Progyny guide also states that **there is growing evidence that certain supplements and micronutrients may help in many ways for those trying to conceive**, but it also emphasizes that **you should be receiving many of your daily vitamins and minerals from food sources** and that supplements should be used after consulting a doctor [N2-F2].

### Which supplements lack strong evidence or are not routinely recommended?
The evidence does not support a strong routine recommendation for many supplements. The Cochrane review explicitly says that **there is insufficient evidence that a specific diet or intake of particular macronutrients can improve natural fertility** [N1-R5]. It also states that **low-quality evidence suggests that there is no difference in live birth or clinical pregnancy rates when comparing a lower dose of melatonin to a higher dose**, and that the overall quality of evidence is limited by serious risks of bias [N1-F1].

Similarly, the evidence for many individual supplements is weak or inconsistent. The Cochrane review found **very low-quality evidence showing no evidence of a difference in clinical pregnancy** and **low quality evidence showing no difference in miscarriage** for the melatonin versus melatonin comparison [N1-F1]. The review also notes that **adverse effects were poorly reported**, and the evidence for safety is therefore limited [N1-F1]. For herbs and unregulated products, the evidence is even thinner: the sources emphasize that herbal supplements are not rigorously evaluated by the FDA, and that **many herbs may have hormone regulatory effects and could cause difficulty conceiving or have harmful effects to pregnancy** [N3-F3].

In short, the strongest evidence is for **folic acid**, while **antioxidants and some other nutrients** may have plausible mechanisms and some suggestive evidence for clinical pregnancy, but **not strong evidence for guaranteed fertility success** [N1-F1][N2-F2]. Most other supplements lack strong evidence, and some are not routinely recommended because the evidence is weak or inconsistent [N1-R5][N1-F1].

## Evidence on safety and side effects

### Common safety concerns for fertility-related supplements
The evidence points to several common safety concerns. First, **herbal supplements are not rigorously evaluated by the FDA**, and the quality and strength of herbal supplements vary between batches and products [N3-F3]. Second, many herbs may contain substances that can cause **miscarriage, premature birth, uterine contractions, or injury to the fetus**, and the evidence base for safety is very limited [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-F3]. Third, some herbs are linked to **specific safety concerns**, including **cannabidiol, chasteberry, red raspberry leaf, rosemary, garlic, saw palmetto, goldenseal, dong quai, ephedra, yohimbe, pay d’arco, passion flower, black cohosh, blue cohosh, roman chamomile, pennyroyal, aloe, ginseng, evening primrose, feverfew, kara kara, senna, angelica, borage oil, mugwort, black walnut, cascara segrada, comfrey, fenugreek, shepherd’s purse, St John’s wort, tansy, ura ursi, and wormwood** [N3-F3].

For general fertility-related supplements, the evidence is still limited. The Cochrane review on vitamins and minerals for female subfertility notes that **adverse effects were poorly reported**, but the use of antioxidants did not appear to lead to more miscarriages, multiple births, digestive effects, or ectopic pregnancies [N1-F1]. It also says the evidence is very low quality, so safety conclusions should be treated cautiously [N1-F1].

### Interactions with medications or other supplements
The evidence emphasizes that **supplements can interact with current medications or existing health conditions in unexpected ways** [N4-F4]. The pharmacist sources specifically warn that **pharmacists can review your medical history and guide you toward options that are safe and effective**, and that **not every supplement is right for every person** [N4-F4]. They also note that **taking the wrong one could do more harm than good**, and that **some supplements contain concentrated nutrients that, if taken in excess, may lead to toxicity or interfere with current medications** [N4-F4].

The pharmacist guidance also highlights that **pharmacists consider diet, activity level, and supplement use**, ensuring these factors align with your personalized health profile [N4-R5]. This is important because the safety and interaction profile of a supplement depends on the individual’s full medication and health context, not just the supplement itself [N4-F4].

### When to avoid or limit a supplement
The evidence supports avoiding or limiting supplements in several situations. First, **herbal supplements should be avoided during pregnancy or while trying to conceive** because some may cause harm, and many are not safe [N3-F3]. Second, **supplements should be used only after consulting a pharmacist or provider**, especially if they are concentrated or may interact with other medications [N4-F4]. Third, **high-dose or concentrated supplements should be approached with caution**, because the evidence suggests that some products may contain harmful levels of nutrients [N4-F4].

The evidence also suggests that **women should start taking multivitamins or prenatal vitamins before getting pregnant**, and that **if a prenatal vitamin doesn’t include some of the standalone vitamins and supplements, they should consult a provider before adding them** [N2-F2]. In other words, rather than starting a supplement regimen independently, the evidence favors **consultation before use** [N2-F2][N4-F4].

Overall, the safety evidence is strongest for **herbal supplements**, where the risk of harm is real and the evidence base is thin [N3-F3]. For other supplements, the evidence supports cautious use, personalized review, and avoiding excessive or unregulated products [N1-F1][N4-F4].

## How to determine the right dosage and whether it should be personalized

### What dosage ranges are supported by evidence?
The evidence does not provide a single fixed dosage for fertility supplements, but it does suggest general ranges based on the available sources. For **folic acid**, the Progyny guide recommends **400–1,000 micrograms for women and 400 micrograms for men**, with methylated folate (quatrefolic) as the preferred form [N2-F2]. For **B12**, the guide suggests **1,000 micrograms once per week for men and women**, and for **B6**, **1.4 milligrams for men and 1.2 milligrams for women daily** [N2-F2]. For **vitamin C**, the guide says **90 milligrams minimum daily for men and 75 milligrams minimum daily for women**, with higher doses up to **2,000 milligrams daily considered safe for most adults** [N2-F2]. For **vitamin D**, the guide recommends **2,000 to 4,000 international units (IU) daily for men and women** [N2-F2]. For **vitamin E**, the guide suggests **mixed tocopherol form, 200–400 IU daily for men and women** [N2-F2]. For **CoQ10**, the evidence is more suggestive than specific, but the guide notes that **CoQ10 is another natural antioxidant that counters oxidative stress that increases with age** and implies a reasonable daily range rather than a specific fixed dose [N2-F2].

These ranges are not universal. The Cochrane review on antioxidants for male subfertility notes that **oral antioxidants were compared with placebo or another antioxidant** in trials, but it does not provide a specific dosage recommendation [N1-R2]. The Cochrane review on vitamins and minerals for female subfertility also includes a wide range of antioxidants and nutrients, but the evidence is low quality and the dosage details are not standardized in the summary [N1-F1]. So the evidence supports **general ranges**, but not a one-size-fits-all dosage.

### Why dose may depend on individual health and lab results
The evidence strongly supports personalization because **not every supplement is right for every person** [N4-F4]. The pharmacist sources emphasize that **pharmacists provide personalized recommendations based on age, health goals, allergies, and medical background** [N4-F4]. They also note that **pharmacists consider diet, activity level, and supplement use**, ensuring these factors align with your personalized health profile [N4-R5]. This is important because a woman’s health status, existing medications, and laboratory results can all affect what is safe and effective.

The Progyny guide also stresses that **you should be receiving many of your daily vitamins and minerals from food sources**, and that **if your prenatal vitamin doesn’t include some of the standalone vitamins and supplements, you might want to consider adding a few to your daily intake after consulting a primary care doctor or your fertility doctor** [N2-F2]. In other words, the decision should not be made in isolation; it should be informed by the individual’s health context and lab results.

### When to consult a provider before taking a supplement
The evidence is clear that consultation is essential. The pharmacist sources state that **pharmacists provide personalized recommendations based on your age, health goals, allergies, and medical background** and that **you should consult a pharmacist before starting a supplement** [N4-F4]. The Progyny guide similarly advises consulting a doctor before adding any supplements to your routine [N2-F2]. The Cochrane review on vitamins and minerals for female subfertility explicitly says that **investigators compared antioxidants with placebo or no treatment/standard treatment**, but it also emphasizes that **adverse effects were poorly reported** and that the evidence is very low quality, so a provider review is especially important [N1-F1].

In short, the evidence supports **consultation before use** because dosage recommendations are not universal and because supplements can interact with medications or health conditions [N4-F4][N2-F2]. The safest approach is to **talk to a pharmacist or provider before starting any new supplement** [N4-F4].

## How to interpret marketing claims and verify supplement ingredients

### What makes a ‘guarantee’ claim suspicious or misleading?
The evidence is very clear that **any product claiming 100% success should be approached with skepticism** [N1-F1][N1-R5]. The Cochrane review on vitamins and minerals for female subfertility explicitly states that **low-quality evidence suggests that antioxidants may improve clinical pregnancy rate compared with placebo or no treatment/standard treatment**, but it was **uncertain whether they improve live birth rates** [N1-F1]. That means **any claim that a supplement guarantees conception is not supported by the evidence** [N1-F1].

The FTC guidance reinforces this point by noting that **the FTC Act does not require pre-market approval of health claims in the advertising of foods, dietary supplements, or other products** [N6-R1]. This means that marketers can make claims without proof, and **guarantee claims are especially misleading** because they promise certainty where the evidence is uncertain [N6-R1].

### How to verify what’s actually in a supplement
The evidence highlights that **herbal supplements are not rigorously evaluated by the FDA**, and that **quality and strength can vary between batches and products** [N3-F3]. The pharmacist sources also note that **pharmacists can review your medical history and guide you toward options that are safe and effective**, and that **pharmacists also consider diet, activity level, and supplement use** [N4-R5]. This implies that the best way to verify a supplement is through **a trusted provider** rather than relying on the product label alone [N4-F4].

The evidence also warns that **some products may contain concentrated nutrients that, if taken in excess, may lead to toxicity or interfere with current medications** [N4-F4]. This means that the actual contents of a supplement may not match the expected dose or ingredient profile. The Progyny guide similarly emphasizes that **not every supplement is right for every person** and that **you should consult a provider before adding a supplement** [N2-F2].

### What steps to take if a product is not properly labeled or appears fraudulent
The evidence suggests a cautious and evidence-based response. First, if a product is not properly labeled, the best step is to **consult a pharmacist or provider** because they can help identify safe and effective options [N4-F4]. Second, if a product appears fraudulent or mislabeled, the pharmacist sources recommend **reviewing your medical history and guiding you toward options that are safe and effective** [N4-F4]. They also emphasize **avoiding overdosing** and **knowing the right dosage** [N4-F4].

The FTC guidance also supports consumer caution by noting that **health claims in advertising are not required to be pre-approved**, which means **misleading claims are possible** [N6-R1]. The supplement mislabeling and false advertising sources further indicate that **the unregulated supplement industry risks consumer health with misleading claims** and that **companies may not test ingredients to confirm their identity before incorporating them into supplements** [N6-R3][N6-R4]. If a product appears fraudulent, the evidence suggests that consumers should **seek trusted sources of information** and **avoid products that promise guaranteed results** [N6-R1][N6-R3].

In short, the evidence supports treating **guarantee claims with skepticism**, **verifying ingredients through a pharmacist or provider**, and **taking action if a product appears mislabeled or unregulated** [N6-R1][N3-F3][N4-F4].

### What dosage ranges are supported by evidence?
The evidence does not provide a single fixed dosage, but it does suggest general ranges based on the available sources.

- **Folic acid**: 400–1,000 micrograms for women, 400 micrograms for men; methylated folate is preferred [N2-F2].
- **B12**: 1,000 micrograms once per week for men and women [N2-F2].

The evidence strongly supports personalization because **not every supplement is right for every person** [N4-F4]. ### What makes a ‘guarantee’ claim suspicious or misleading?
The evidence is very clear that **any product claiming 100% success should be approached with skepticism** [N1-F1][N1-R5]. ## Evidence on which supplements may help fertility

### Which supplements have plausible biological mechanisms for fertility?
The evidence base supports a few supplements based on plausible biological mechanisms, particularly antioxidants and nutrients involved in reproductive health. Cochrane reviews and fertility guides highlight that antioxidants are thought to reduce oxidative stress, which may be relevant to fertility outcomes [N1-F1]. This is why the Cochrane review on vitamins and minerals for female subfertility explicitly included antioxidants and related compounds such as N-acetylcysteine, melatonin, L-arginine, myo-inositol, carnitine, selenium, vitamin E, vitamin B complex, vitamin C, vitamin D+calcium, CoQ10, and omega-3-polyunsaturated fatty acids [N1-F1].

Folic acid also has a clear biological rationale: it is associated with greater chances of getting pregnant naturally and is a core recommendation for women trying to conceive [N2-F2]. Vitamin B6 and B12 are also linked to hormonal balance and ovulatory cycles in women, and some studies suggest they may improve conception odds [N2-F2]. Myo-inositol and D-chiro-inositol are tied to insulin and gonadotropin signaling, affecting follicle maturation and are especially relevant for women with PCOS [N2-F2]. Vitamin C is a powerful antioxidant that may reduce free radical damage and counter aspects of ovarian aging [N2-F2]. Vitamin D is important for hormone development and may improve pregnancy rates, while vitamin E improves reproductive health and egg quality [N2-F2]. CoQ10 is another antioxidant that counters oxidative stress and is promoted for egg and sperm quality [N2-F2].

### Which supplements have moderate evidence for improving pregnancy rates?
The evidence for improving pregnancy rates is more modest than for some of the mechanisms. For antioxidants, the Cochrane review found **low-quality evidence suggesting that antioxidants may improve clinical pregnancy rates compared with placebo or no treatment/standard treatment**, but it was **uncertain whether they improve live birth rates** [N1-F1]. The same review also noted that the evidence was very low quality overall, with serious risks of bias, poor reporting, imprecision, and inconsistency [N1-F1]. A subsequent source also notes that **CoQ10 has shown potential to increase clinical pregnancy rates but has not shown significant increase in live birth rates** [N2-R2].

For folic acid, the evidence is more direct: the Cochrane review explicitly states that **daily folic acid supplementation in ...** is part of the review, and the Progyny guide notes that **folic acid is associated with greater chances of getting pregnant naturally and improves success for those undergoing fertility treatments** [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The evidence for folic acid is therefore stronger than for many antioxidants, though still not a guaranteed fertility guarantee.

For other supplements, the evidence is less robust. The Cochrane review on vitamins and minerals for female subfertility included 63 trials, but the overall quality was very low, and the results were uncertain for live birth and only suggestive for clinical pregnancy [N1-F1]. The evidence on specific supplements such as melatonin, N-acetylcysteine, and L-carnitine is similarly limited by very low quality [N1-F1]. The Progyny guide also states that **there is growing evidence that certain supplements and micronutrients may help in many ways for those trying to conceive**, but it also emphasizes that **you should be receiving many of your daily vitamins and minerals from food sources** and that supplements should be used after consulting a doctor [N2-F2].

### Which supplements lack strong evidence or are not routinely recommended?
The evidence does not support a strong routine recommendation for many supplements. The Cochrane review explicitly says that **there is insufficient evidence that a specific diet or intake of particular macronutrients can improve natural fertility** [N1-R5]. It also states that **low-quality evidence suggests that there is no difference in live birth or clinical pregnancy rates when comparing a lower dose of melatonin to a higher dose**, and that the overall quality of evidence is limited by serious risks of bias [N1-F1].

Similarly, the evidence for many individual supplements is weak or inconsistent. The Cochrane review found **very low-quality evidence showing no evidence of a difference in clinical pregnancy** and **low quality evidence showing no difference in miscarriage** for the melatonin versus melatonin comparison [N1-F1]. The review also notes that **adverse effects were poorly reported**, and the evidence for safety is therefore limited [N1-F1]. For herbs and unregulated products, the evidence is even thinner: the sources emphasize that herbal supplements are not rigorously evaluated by the FDA, and that **many herbs may have hormone regulatory effects and could cause difficulty conceiving or have harmful effects to pregnancy** [N3-F3].

In short, the strongest evidence is for **folic acid**, while **antioxidants and some other nutrients** may have plausible mechanisms and some suggestive evidence for clinical pregnancy, but **not strong evidence for guaranteed fertility success** [N1-F1][N2-F2]. Most other supplements lack strong evidence, and some are not routinely recommended because the evidence is weak or inconsistent [N1-R5][N1-F1].

### Common safety concerns for fertility-related supplements
The evidence points to several common safety concerns. First, **herbal supplements are not rigorously evaluated by the FDA**, and the quality and strength of herbal supplements vary between batches and products [N3-F3]. For general fertility-related supplements, the evidence is still limited. The Cochrane review on vitamins and minerals for female subfertility notes that **adverse effects were poorly reported**, but the use of antioxidants did not appear to lead to more miscarriages, multiple births, digestive effects, or ectopic pregnancies [N1-F1]. It also says the evidence is very low quality, so safety conclusions should be treated cautiously [N1-F1].

### Interactions with medications or other supplements
The evidence emphasizes that **supplements can interact with current medications or existing health conditions in unexpected ways** [N4-F4]. The pharmacist guidance also highlights that **pharmacists consider diet, activity level, and supplement use**, ensuring these factors align with your personalized health profile [N4-R5]. This is important because the safety and interaction profile of a supplement depends on the individual’s full medication and health context, not just the supplement itself [N4-F4].

### When to avoid or limit a supplement
The evidence supports avoiding or limiting supplements in several situations. First, **herbal supplements should be avoided during pregnancy or while trying to conceive** because some may cause harm, and many are not safe [N3-F3]. Second, **supplements should be used only after consulting a pharmacist or provider**, especially if they are concentrated or may interact with other medications [N4-F4]. Third, **high-dose or concentrated supplements should be approached with caution**, because the evidence suggests that some products may contain harmful levels of nutrients [N4-F4].

The evidence base supports a few supplements based on plausible biological mechanisms, particularly antioxidants and nutrients involved in reproductive health. Myo-inositol and D-chiro-inositol are tied to insulin and gonadotropin signaling, affecting follicle maturation and are especially relevant for women with PCOS [N2-F2]. Vitamin C is a powerful antioxidant that may reduce free radical damage and counter aspects of ovarian aging [N2-F2]. Vitamin D is important for hormone development and may improve pregnancy rates, while vitamin E improves reproductive health and egg quality [N2-F2]. CoQ10 is another antioxidant that counters oxidative stress and is promoted for egg and sperm quality [N2-F2].

### Which supplements have moderate evidence for improving pregnancy rates?
The evidence for improving pregnancy rates is more modest than for some of the mechanisms. For antioxidants, the Cochrane review found **low-quality evidence suggesting that antioxidants may improve clinical pregnancy rates compared with placebo or no treatment/standard treatment**, but it was **uncertain whether they improve live birth rates** [N1-F1]. The same review also noted that the evidence was very low quality overall, with serious risks of bias, poor reporting, imprecision, and inconsistency [N1-F1]. A subsequent source also notes that **CoQ10 has shown potential to increase clinical pregnancy rates but has not shown significant increase in live birth rates** [N2-R2].

The evidence for folic acid is therefore stronger than for many antioxidants, though still not a guaranteed fertility guarantee.

For other supplements, the evidence is less robust. The Cochrane review on vitamins and minerals for female subfertility included 63 trials, but the overall quality was very low, and the results were uncertain for live birth and only suggestive for clinical pregnancy [N1-F1]. The evidence on specific supplements such as melatonin, N-acetylcysteine, and L-carnitine is similarly limited by very low quality [N1-F1]. The Progyny guide also states that **there is growing evidence that certain supplements and micronutrients may help in many ways for those trying to conceive**, but it also emphasizes that **you should be receiving many of your daily vitamins and minerals from food sources** and that supplements should be used after consulting a doctor [N2-F2].

### Common safety concerns for fertility-related supplements
The evidence points to several common safety concerns. First, **herbal supplements are not rigorously evaluated by the FDA**, and the quality and strength of herbal supplements vary between batches and products [N3-F3]. The evidence emphasizes that **supplements can interact with current medications or existing health conditions in unexpected ways** [N4-F4]. The pharmacist guidance also highlights that **pharmacists consider diet, activity level, and supplement use**, ensuring these factors align with your personalized health profile [N4-R5]. The evidence supports avoiding or limiting supplements in several situations.
